evaluation.positioning_hook: A bullied teen clique’s prank on a dead classmate boomerangs into a masked-killer bloodbath, as secrets, crushes, and betrayals turn a high school friend group into prey.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The core promise is easy to grasp: teen friendship, betrayal, and a killer stalking a school circle. The audience lane is clear, though the script’s sprawling cast and repeated relationship turns make the commercial pitch more specific than broad.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The murder mystery and revenge engine are legible early, especially once Katie’s death and the friend-group fallout land. The hook is there, but the script keeps adding new relationship permutations and family threads before the central killer question fully locks in.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sammy, Lucy, Faye, Austin, and Lauren all have distinct social energy, and the script gives them strong behavioral signatures. At the same time, many of the characters are defined more by volume, romance, or attitude than by a single durable contradiction, so the ensemble plays more as functional than iconic.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to teen melodrama, but the setup leans on familiar slasher and friend-group betrayal mechanics. The boldest choice is the sheer scale of interpersonal chaos, yet the underlying structure stays close to recognizable genre beats.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps moving through deaths, interrogations, parties, and confrontations, so there is always another event on deck. The momentum is more cumulative than escalating, though, because the script repeatedly resets into new social scenes before the killer engine fully tightens.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a teen friend group collapsing under a revenge killing spree has immediate genre familiarity. The specific social texture around talkative Faye, party-girl Sammy, and the romance web gives it some flavor, but not yet a singular premise that feels inevitable and new.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The school, homes, police station, and party spaces create a recognizable teen ecosystem with parents, teachers, and cops all entering the pressure cooker. The world is active, but it functions more as a stage for events than as a deeply rule-bound social system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a consistent heightened teen-horror tone, with comic banter, romance, and sudden brutality living in the same space. That said, the tone often swings between soap-opera intimacy and explicit slasher violence without a fully singular signature voice.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of deeper material in Lucy’s insecurity, Sammy’s need for validation, and the group’s cruelty toward Katie. The script gestures toward those reserves, but most of the emotional material is stated directly rather than held back for discovery.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is the script’s strongest structural asset: nearly every scene is powered by shifting pairings, jealousies, and alliances. Sammy/Lucy, Austin/Lauren/Julia, and Faye/Daniel all generate usable story energy, and the ensemble keeps producing new combinations.

casting_characteristics: one police officer with recurring presence

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical blood and body-impact work; no major effects world, but repeated gore, wounds, and death beats require consistent makeup and blood rigs.
technical.sfx_needs: Knife attacks, chokeholds, falls, gunshots, and repeated injury choreography across multiple attack scenes.

rights_flags.detail: Vape use is depicted generically but not brand-specific.
Get Out is specifically named and discussed on screen.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: festival-to-platform or direct streaming genre play

cost.note: Contemporary teen settings keep the footprint manageable, but the script uses multiple homes, a school, a police station, a restaurant, a park, repeated night work, and several gore-heavy attack sequences.

cast.note: The story leans on a large teen ensemble plus parents, a teacher, a cop, a janitor, and an elderly antagonist, with several roles needing strong chemistry to land.

location.note: The setting is contemporary and mostly domestic, but the script moves through many distinct interiors and exteriors, including multiple houses, school spaces, and a park.

content.note: The script includes repeated graphic killings, bloodshed, choking, throat slits, gunshots, profanity, teen sexuality, and drug/vape use.

rights.note: The script names Get Out, McDonald’s, and DoorDash directly, which creates some clearance and brand-consideration work.

strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of cast web that can carry a feature because every pairing has friction, flirtation, or betrayal baked in. Teen-thriller buyers and actors who like group dynamics will respond to how often the script finds a new social angle inside the same pressure cooker.
strengths.evidence: Sammy/Lucy’s friendship fracture, Austin/Lauren/Julia’s triangle, and Faye/Daniel’s hyper-verbal couple scenes all create separate engines.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Sammy is a strong central engine.
strengths.what_it_means: Sammy has the right mix of social confidence, defensiveness, and emotional volatility to anchor a slasher franchise or a one-off feature. Casting directors will see a role that can play funny, messy, romantic, and furious in the same movie.
strengths.evidence: She parties hard, deflects in the police interview, and then becomes the emotional center of the final confrontation with Ryan and Lucy.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Lucy has a real transformation arc.
strengths.what_it_means: Lucy’s shift from withdrawn outsider to explosive antagonist to remorseful ally gives the movie a performance lane with real range. That kind of part attracts actors who want a visible emotional turn and a final-act redemption beat.
strengths.evidence: Her cafeteria blowup, her insecurity confession in the house, and her return to save Sammy from Ryan all mark distinct phases.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The teen romance web is highly playable.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives the movie a built-in audience hook beyond the kills: crushes, breakups, jealousy, and loyalty tests keep the emotional stakes active between horror beats. That makes it attractive to buyers looking for genre with relationship heat and to young ensemble actors who want chemistry-driven material.
strengths.evidence: Austin/Lauren/Julia, Sammy/Ryan, and Faye/Daniel all get extended romantic scenes and reversals.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The killer reveal is structurally usable.
strengths.what_it_means: The Ryan reveal gives the story a clean revenge motive tied back to Katie, which is exactly the kind of late-turn genre payoff that can land with audiences. It also gives the film a marketable mystery spine that can be sold on the question of who is behind the mask.
strengths.evidence: Ryan is revealed as the hooded killer and explains his motive through Katie’s death and the prank fallout.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script is producible in contemporary spaces.
strengths.what_it_means: This is a horror feature that can be mounted without period builds or large-scale world effects, which keeps it in a practical indie-to-streaming lane. Buyers who like contained contemporary genre pieces will see a path to execution without a giant footprint.
strengths.evidence: Most scenes take place in houses, school interiors, a bathroom, a cafeteria, a police station, and a park.

whats_special.headline: This script has a real ensemble engine: the friend-group dynamics are messy, specific, and constantly generating new conflict, which is exactly what a teen slasher needs to keep moving. The Sammy/Lucy center of gravity, the Austin/Lauren/Julia triangle, and the eventual Ryan reveal give the project a marketable mix of romance, betrayal, and revenge that can play to horror buyers and young-cast audiences alike.

lead_characters.name: Sammy Miller
lead_characters.hook: Sammy is the social center of the group: party-forward, sharp-tongued, defensive when cornered, and emotionally messier than she admits. She wants control, fun, and loyalty, but the script keeps forcing her to confront the damage inside her own circle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the volatility of Maika Monroe in The Guest and the social command of a teen lead in a prestige ensemble. It offers the showcase of playing a character who can be funny, wounded, accusatory, and finally survival-driven without losing the room.

lead_characters.name: Lucy Carmen
lead_characters.hook: Lucy starts as the quiet observer, then detonates into a bitter, isolated teen who feels invisible inside her own friend group. Under the anger is a deep need to be chosen, and the script eventually lets that need surface as remorse and loyalty.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a performance like Jena Malone in Donnie Darko or Sophie Thatcher in Yellowjackets, where the character’s interior fracture becomes the engine of the role. It gives an actor the chance to play repression, humiliation, rage, and redemption in one part.

lead_characters.name: Austin Moore
lead_characters.hook: Austin is the polished, confident social operator who thinks he can manage every room with charm and logic. He’s romantic, status-aware, and often self-satisfied, which makes him useful as both a stabilizer and a source of friction.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that lets an actor do the charismatic teen lead work seen in performances like Logan Lerman in The Perks of Being a Wallflower, but with more swagger and social control. It offers the chance to play charm as a mask and then let that mask crack under pressure.

lead_characters.name: Lauren Cheng
lead_characters.hook: Lauren is observant, emotionally literate, and often the calmest person in the room, which gives her a quiet authority inside the group. She’s also deeply invested in romance and loyalty, so her composure carries a private ache.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded teen role that gives an actor the measured emotional intelligence of a performance like Auli’i Cravalho in The Power or Hailee Steinfeld in early ensemble work. The showcase is subtlety: listening, withholding, and then landing emotional truth in a group scene.

lead_characters.name: Faye Woodbridge
lead_characters.hook: Faye is loud, theatrical, needy, funny, and impossible to ignore, with a mouth that runs ahead of her self-awareness. She’s built as a comic pressure valve, but the script also gives her real grief and panic, which makes her more than just the chatterbox of the group.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the big, scene-stealing volatility of a performance like Kaitlyn Dever in Booksmart, but with a more openly heightened horror-melodrama edge. It offers a showcase for rapid-fire comedy, emotional collapse, and physical survival.

lead_characters.name: Daniel Stokes-Simpson
lead_characters.hook: Daniel is the smooth, supportive boyfriend archetype who tries to manage everyone’s energy and keep the group calm. He’s affectionate and socially fluent, which makes him feel like the glue until the violence starts stripping that away.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the likable, emotionally legible boyfriend slot seen in performances like Noah Centineo in teen ensemble work, but with a darker horror payoff. The showcase is playing warmth and control before the script turns him into a victim with real emotional weight.

lead_characters.name: Eric Smith
lead_characters.hook: Eric is the quiet outsider who watches more than he speaks, which makes him feel both vulnerable and hard to read. He’s the least socially loud person in the group, but that stillness gives him a distinct presence when the story turns dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the reserved, emotionally guarded lane of a performance like Justice Smith in ensemble drama. It offers the showcase of saying very little and still carrying tension, then landing a late emotional turn.

lead_characters.name: Ryan
lead_characters.hook: Ryan presents as the new quiet guy with a soft edge, then reveals himself as the story’s revenge engine and final predator. He’s a classic bait-and-switch role: charming enough to disarm the group, dangerous enough to reframe the whole movie.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of reveal role that gives an actor the late-turn menace of a performance like Jack Quaid in a horror twist, but with more direct villain monologue space. The showcase is the transformation from low-key romantic interest to masked killer with motive.

lead_characters.name: Katie Davis
lead_characters.hook: Katie is the absent center of the story: the dead classmate whose murder and social humiliation set the whole chain in motion. She functions as the emotional and moral ghost haunting the friend group.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a brief but memorable presence in the opening, similar to the catalytic victim roles in slashers that define the whole movie. The showcase is in making the audience feel the loss before the story turns into revenge.

lead_characters.name: Katie’s Mom
lead_characters.hook: Katie’s mom is the warm, ordinary parent whose brief presence makes the opening attack hit harder. She represents the domestic normalcy the movie is about to destroy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of short but emotionally loaded role that gives an actor the grounded parent beat seen in opening-victim material from slashers and thrillers. The showcase is making a small amount of screen time feel devastating.

lead_characters.name: Sammy’s Grandma
lead_characters.hook: Sammy’s grandma is the unstable, recurring threat figure who appears as both warning and violence. She carries the movie’s older-generation menace and gives the story its first direct physical predator.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the unhinged antagonist energy of a horror matriarch or stalker figure. The showcase is playing volatility, menace, and physical threat in a way that can dominate every scene she enters.

lead_characters.name: Officer Wilson
lead_characters.hook: Officer Wilson is the procedural pressure valve: skeptical, blunt, and often more adversarial than helpful. He gives the story an institutional face and a way to externalize suspicion inside the school-town ecosystem.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the hard-edged authority of a procedural cop with a personal stake, similar to the grounded law-enforcement lane in teen thrillers. The showcase is playing interrogation scenes that carry both tension and attitude.

lead_characters.name: Ms. Johnson
lead_characters.hook: Ms. Johnson is the school authority voice who frames the deaths and keeps the institutional world moving. She’s functional but important as the adult system reacting to the chaos.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the efficient authority beat of a teacher in a genre ensemble. The showcase is delivering exposition and emotional punctuation with clarity.

lead_characters.name: Anala
lead_characters.hook: Anala is Julia’s mother, a warm but blunt parent who helps define the family world around the teens. She gives the movie a domestic counterpoint to the school chaos.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded parent material seen in family scenes inside teen thrillers. The showcase is playing warmth, exasperation, and protective instinct in a compact space.

lead_characters.name: Viraj
lead_characters.hook: Viraj is the calm father figure in Julia’s home, present as part of the family texture rather than as a plot driver. He helps make the domestic world feel lived in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the steady-parent lane often used to ground a teen ensemble. The showcase is understated authority and family realism.

lead_characters.name: Rohan
lead_characters.hook: Rohan is Julia’s younger brother, part of the family stakes that make the home invasion land harder. He functions as a vulnerable domestic presence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small role that gives a young performer a clear emotional function in a horror setup. The showcase is being part of the family texture that the audience feels before the attack.

lead_characters.name: Naomi
lead_characters.hook: Naomi is Lauren’s mother, a supportive adult who helps anchor Lauren’s home life. She adds warmth and normalcy to the ensemble’s off-campus world.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the reassuring parent beat in a teen ensemble. The showcase is emotional steadiness and maternal support.

lead_characters.name: Ken
lead_characters.hook: Ken is part of Lauren’s family unit and functions as background domestic support. He helps round out the home environment.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting parent role that gives an actor a clean family-scene presence. The showcase is simple, believable domesticity.

lead_characters.name: James
lead_characters.hook: James appears as part of Lauren’s family scene and helps establish the household as a real place with multiple moving parts. He is a texture character rather than a plot engine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small family role that gives an actor a quick, readable presence in a genre ensemble. The showcase is naturalistic household energy.

lead_characters.name: Sarah
lead_characters.hook: Sarah is Lucy’s younger sibling, used to sharpen the cruelty of Lucy’s home life. She functions as a domestic contrast to Lucy’s isolation.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that gives a young performer a clear emotional function in a family scene. The showcase is being the innocent counterpoint to the older sibling’s distress.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to turn teen social chaos into a blood-soaked pressure cooker.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature horror directors, or indie filmmakers moving up from shorts, who already like ensemble behavior, contained locations, and performance-forward genre. This material rewards someone who can keep the camera close to shifting alliances, then pay them off with clean, visceral attack scenes.
director_appeal.detail: The movie lives or dies on timing, chemistry, and tonal control more than on spectacle, which makes it a strong fit for a director who can stage dialogue scenes like mini confrontations. The right filmmaker gets a cast-heavy horror feature with enough emotional movement to feel bigger than its footprint.

buyer_appeal.detail: The project can be cast around a strong teen ensemble rather than a single expensive star, which helps it package off chemistry and concept. The revenge-slasher lane remains a reliable streaming buy-zone, and the contemporary school/home footprint keeps it exportable and producible without period or franchise baggage.

considerations.detail: The Katie attack is the movie’s cleanest hook, and the version of the script where it gets to the point a little sooner would put the audience into the engine earlier. Right now the domestic setup is clear, but a tighter lead-in would make the first kill feel like the true launch rather than a long prelude.

Several cafeteria and hangout sequences repeat the same social function: who likes whom, who is annoyed, who is hiding something. One lever would be to let a few of those scenes collapse into sharper turns so the movie keeps its momentum while preserving the ensemble chemistry.

considerations.area: The killer reveal can be seeded earlier.
considerations.detail: Ryan’s late reveal works as a payoff, but the script would gain more charge if his presence carried a few more unsettling details before the mask comes off. A few earlier behavioral tells would make the final turn feel even more inevitable.

There are a lot of named teens, parents, and authority figures, which gives the movie texture but also asks for a lot of casting coordination. A streamlined version that folds a couple of the adult functions together would protect the ensemble energy while making the package easier to assemble.

considerations.area: The gore level defines the lane.
considerations.detail: The repeated throat slits, stabbings, chokeholds, and head trauma place this firmly in mature horror territory. That clarity helps the buyer conversation, but it also means the script is best positioned with platforms and distributors that actively want explicit genre content.

considerations.area: Brand and title references need a pass.
considerations.detail: Get Out, McDonald’s, and DoorDash are all named directly, so a production-ready version would want a quick clearance review. The good news is that none of those references are structurally essential, so they can be adjusted without changing the story engine.
